name: Yemen
sources: THE UNIFICATION, STATED FIRST BECAUSE EVERYTHING ELSE DEPENDS ON IT. On 1 January 1990, when this game opens, there was no Republic of Yemen. There were two states: the Yemen Arab Republic in Sanaa, a market economy of about 9.7m people under Ali Abdullah Saleh, and the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen in Aden, the only Marxist-Leninist state in the Arab world, about 2.4m people, whose ruling party had destroyed itself in the twelve-day civil war of January 1986. They merged on 22 May 1990. This roster carries the unified Republic from January, four months and three weeks early, and the reason is structural rather than lazy: SPHERES creates successor states when a federation comes apart and has no machinery for the reverse, BIBLE section 5 refuses the scripted event that would be the alternative, and entering two Yemens would leave one of them permanently on the board as a country that ceased to exist in the game's first year. The four-month offset is the smallest available distortion and it is disclosed rather than smoothed over.

GDP $12.64bn - THIS FIGURE IS ENTERED UNDER PROTEST AND IS THE FIRST ENTRY IN THIS BRANCH'S UNVERIFIED LIST. It is World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, series YEM, 1990 - $12,643,821,568.96 - and it is the series every other 1990 GDP in this roster sits on, which is the only argument for it. Three independent checks say it is wrong by a factor of about two, and they are stated in full because the alternative is a number I made up. FIRST: the same series runs 12.6 (1990), 14.7, 18.0, 21.7, 28.0 (1994), then 12.8 (1995) and 6.5 (1996). Yemen's real economy did not shrink by 77% in two years; what happened is that the 1995-96 IMF programme floated the rial from an official 12 to the dollar to about 130, and everything before 1995 in that series is an official-rate conversion that the Bank's own later prints disown. SECOND: the Bank publishes no Atlas GNI per capita for Yemen in 1990 at all, having declined to classify it - the only nation in this branch for which that is true. THIRD, and decisively: the Bank's own NY.GDP.PETR.RT.ZS puts Yemeni oil rents at 28.51% of GDP in 1990, which on this denominator is $3.60bn of rent against 70.4m barrels of annual production - $51 a barrel of pure rent in a year when oil averaged $23. That is arithmetically impossible, and inverting it implies a GDP nearer $5-6bn. A GDP of $12.64bn also puts Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, above Syria and level with Oman in the league table, which is visibly wrong on the board. It is carried anyway because the recipe's convention is one series for comparability and because every substitute I could compute would be my arithmetic rather than anybody's measurement. FLAGGED FOR THE INTEGRATOR: this is the one figure in this branch I would change if a sourced alternative appeared.

Population 13.89m: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series YEM, 1990 - 13,887,862. This series is already the combined republic in 1990, which is convenient and is also a small piece of evidence for the choice made above: the World Bank itself treats 1990 as the unified state's first year.

TFP trend 0.006: level with Iran's, above Iraq's and Lebanon's 0.005. Yemen in 1990 had almost no manufacturing, an agriculture increasingly given over to qat, and an economy whose largest single input was the remittances of roughly a million Yemenis working in Saudi Arabia - a flow Riyadh cut off in September 1990 in retaliation for Sanaa's refusal to condemn the invasion of Kuwait, expelling some 800,000 of them.

Inflation 30% - FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED AND ESTIMATED, NOT TRANSCRIBED. No 1990 consumer price print exists for either Yemen: the World Bank's FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG is null and the IMF series for the unified republic begins in 1991 at 44.9%, rising to 51.2% in 1992. That 1991 print cannot honestly be moved back a year, because most of it is the consequence of an event that had not happened in January 1990 - the mass return of expelled workers and the loss of Saudi and Gulf budget support after August. 0.30 is placed between the low-twenties inflation the Yemen Arab Republic reported in the late 1980s and that 1991 print. It is an estimate, it is stated as one, and it is in the unverified list.

Interest rate 13% - FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED. Neither FR.INR.LEND nor FR.INR.DPST has a 1990 value for Yemen. Rates were administered by the Central Bank of Yemen rather than set by a market, and were deeply negative in real terms throughout this period, which is the property being represented: 0.13 against 0.30 inflation is a real rate of about minus seventeen percent. Not a print.

Revenue 20% of GDP - FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED. No World Bank revenue series for Yemen in 1990. 0.20 is placed level with Egypt's shipped 0.20 and below Syria's 0.22, on the reasoning that Yemen's treasury took the oil royalty on 193,000 b/d, customs at Aden and Hodeidah, and little else - and note that the denominator problem in the GDP entry above cuts both ways here.

Military 6.6% of GDP: World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS (SIPRI basis), series YEM, 1990 - 6.55118344395031. Transcribed, and a caution about it: this is a share of the disputed GDP denominator, so the dollar amount it implies inherits that problem even though the ratio is published.

Public investment 7.2% and private investment 3.3% of GDP: World Bank NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS gives total gross fixed capital formation of 10.5043323105206% and NE.GDI.FPRV.ZS gives the private share as 3.31580583679152%, leaving the state 7.19%. Both transcribed. Private capital formation of 3.3% of GDP is the lowest in this branch and is what an economy running on remittances and imports rather than on domestic accumulation looks like.

Debt 51% of GDP: World Bank DT.DOD.DECT.GN.ZS, series YEM, 1990 - 50.5753197786632% of GNI, on external debt stocks of $6,354,026,972.50 (DT.DOD.DECT.CD). The dollar debt figure is solid; the ratio is not, for the reason given above - against the Bank's own first market-rate GDP print of $6.50bn in 1996 the same debt is 98% of output. The published ratio is entered and the caveat is stated. Most of that stock was Soviet arms credit to Aden and Chinese and Gulf project lending to Sanaa.

Oil 193,000 barrels a day: EIA international crude production, Yemen, 1990 - 193 thousand b/d, against 194 in 1989 and 197 in 1991. Yemen had only just become a producer: Hunt Oil found the Alif field in the Marib-Jawf basin of the north in 1984 and the export pipeline opened in 1987, and Canadian Occidental's Masila field in the south's Hadhramaut came on stream in 1993. That the oil straddles the old north-south line, in a country where each side's army was still its own, is not a small detail.

Stability 40 and authoritarianism 0.55: stability is set below Iraq's 48 because the state that existed in 1990 was an agreement between two governments rather than a government. The unification of 22 May put a five-man Presidential Council over a merged cabinet, but the two armies were never integrated - the northern forces stayed under Saleh's officers and the southern under the Yemeni Socialist Party's - and the arrangement ended in the civil war of May to July 1994, when the south seceded as the Democratic Republic of Yemen and was reconquered. Authoritarianism 0.55 is set deliberately below the ELECTORAL_CEILING of 0.60, level with Jordan's and Pakistan's, and the justification is the most surprising fact about this period in Arabian politics: the unification agreement legalised parties, freed the press, and produced the parliamentary election of 27 April 1993, the first free multiparty election ever held on the Arabian peninsula. Sanaa in 1990-93 was more open than any of its neighbours. It did not last.

Separatism 0.50: below the USSR's 0.55 and Yugoslavia's 0.72, above Israel's 0.40. The south did secede, on 21 May 1994, and unlike Yugoslavia's republics it was defeated and reabsorbed within ten weeks - which is exactly the difference the ordering encodes: a separatism that produced a war and no new state.

Military strength 4.0: level with the UAE's 4.0 and below Jordan's 6.0. The combined force was about 65,000 men with a large stock of Soviet equipment inherited from both sides - T-54s and T-55s, MiG-21s, a handful of MiG-29s ordered by Sanaa - which is more metal than Jordan had. It is not indexed above Jordan because two armies that will not merge and that answer to rival parties are worth less than one army that answers to one king, and the 1994 war is the demonstration.

pop_growth_1990 = 3.9221%/yr. Compound annual growth of World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series YEM (Yemen, Rep.): 11,025,597 in 1984 to 13,364,174 in 1989 — the five years ending on the eve of the 1 January 1990 start date. See EconomyRecord::pop_growth_1990 in spheres-sim/src/data/mod.rs for why the window ends in 1989 and not with the single-year 1990 rate.

note: 1990 TECHNOLOGY: AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED. What this nation knew on 1 January 1990 is transcribed and sourced grant by grant, exactly like every other 1990 figure in this file, and is not read off tfp_trend - there was never a code path from the trend to the known set, and the zero that stood there was a claim about the world rather than an absence of one (BIBLE section 8 and iron rule 4, both amended 2026-08-30). THE PREDICATE IS SPLIT, and split by the technology's OWN EFFECT TYPE so that it is mechanically computable and never a per-nation judgement call. A node whose effects include MilitaryEfficiency, MilitaryStrength, DiffusionEmission or CostReduction is SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE: holding it means this nation could PRODUCE it, so operating an imported article does not qualify. Every other node is USE-SIDE: deployed and in operational use here is enough, whoever built it, because the effect such a node pays is a productivity, health or output effect and that effect is real in the country where the machine runs. Of the 48 technologies the tree lets anyone hold in 1990, 17 are sovereignty-side and 31 are use-side.

DATA-KEYED TAIL NATION. This nation is outside the 29 authored majors, so nothing here was authored technology by technology: a grant is made only where one of two named published global series supports it, and nothing is modelled, estimated or interpolated. A short list, or an empty one, is the correct outcome of that rule and not a gap in the work.

Data-keyed tail nation: not one of the 29 authored majors. Only the two series named in ruling 3 were consulted - WHO/UNICEF WUENIC DTP3 1990 and World Bank IT.CEL.SETS. Nothing was modelled, estimated or interpolated, and no other evidence was admitted. ISO3 key used for both series: YEM.
WUENIC DTP3 1990 = 84% against the 80% UCI-1990 threshold: bio_universal_immunisation GRANTED.
IT.CEL.SETS at 31 December 1989 = 0 against a threshold of any positive count: refused.

The other 46 grantable 1990 technologies are BLANK for this nation by design, not by oversight: the 17 sovereignty-side entries are unreachable by any use-in-operation series, and no published global series was named that keys the remaining 29 use-side entries.

granted.source: WHO/UNICEF WUENIC DTP3 immunisation coverage (% of surviving infants), retrieved from the UNICEF public SDMX API, dataflow UNICEF:IMMUNISATION(1.0), indicator IM_DTP3, DATA_SOURCE field 'WHO/UNICEF estimates of national immunization coverage, 2025 revision'. Series value: YEM, 1990 = 84%, at or above the 80% WHO/UNICEF Universal Childhood Immunization (UCI-1990) target that defines this technology's name. The 1989 value of the same series is 56%, on the other side of the 80% line: THRESHOLD-SENSITIVE CELL.
